title: Why do we yawn
paragraphs: Yawning is something we all do – maybe because we’re bored carrying out tedious tasks or because we’re tired. Sometimes, just seeing other people yawn can set you off. But is this biological function really contagious, and why do we do it in the first place?

Many of us think we open our mouths when we yawn to take in more oxygen, but in fact it appears there is no clear biological reason. According to BBC Bitesize, new research suggests it might be because yawning cools the brain down and prevents it from overheating, much like the fan in your laptop. This might be why we’re more likely to feel drowsy and yawn in warm temperatures.

What is clear is that we yawn more when we’re exhausted and ready for a nap, and we can’t control when we do it – once we start, there’s no stopping us! But it’s also true that yawning is a very contagious behaviour. John Drury, a researcher from Sussex University, told the BBC that “it’s meant to be automatic; it’s something that you can’t stop. Dogs yawn when their owners yawn, animals yawn to each other. It happens whether you want to or not.”

His research into this cognitive behaviour found that there is a connection with our social group and how close we are to the people in it. If we identify with the person who exhibits the behaviour, we are likely to copy it too.

Other research by the University of Nottingham in 2017 found similar results. They asked volunteers to watch other people yawn. They found their ability to resist yawning when others around them yawned was limited. And the urge to yawn was increased when people were told they couldn’t. They also found, when using electrical stimulation, that they were able to increase people’s desire to yawn. These findings, they say, could be useful because it could help treat other conditions like Tourette’s, which involve the same area of the brain.
What is certain is that a yawn can creep up on us at any time even when we think we’re not tired – but, I hope, not when you’re reading this article!

vocabulary.entry: yawn /jɔːn/ v. 打哈欠 n. 哈欠
vocabulary.example: She gave a big yawn and stretched after waking up.
vocabulary.translation: 她醒来后打了个大哈欠，伸了个懒腰。

vocabulary.entry: tedious /ˈtiːdiəs/ adj. 单调乏味的；冗长的
vocabulary.example: The meeting was long and tedious, with no real progress.
vocabulary.translation: 这个会议冗长乏味，没有取得任何实质性进展。

vocabulary.entry: set off /set ɒf/ 引发；触发（某种反应）
vocabulary.example: The sound of thunder set off a panic among the children.
vocabulary.translation: 雷声引发了孩子们的恐慌。

vocabulary.entry: biological function /ˌbaɪəˈlɒdʒɪkl ˈfʌŋkʃn/ 生理功能
vocabulary.example: Breathing is a basic biological function necessary for life.
vocabulary.translation: 呼吸是维持生命所必需的基本生理功能。

vocabulary.entry: contagious /kənˈteɪdʒəs/ adj. （行为、情绪）有感染力的；传染的
vocabulary.example: Her smile is so contagious that everyone around her feels happy.
vocabulary.translation: 她的笑容很有感染力，周围的人都感到开心。

vocabulary.entry: take in /teɪk ɪn/ 吸入；吸收
vocabulary.example: Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
vocabulary.translation: 植物吸入二氧化碳，释放氧气。

vocabulary.entry: oxygen /ˈɒksɪdʒən/ n. 氧气
vocabulary.example: We need oxygen to survive, which we get from the air.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要氧气才能生存，氧气来自空气。

vocabulary.entry: cool down /kuːl daʊn/ 降温；冷却
vocabulary.example: Let the soup cool down before you eat it.
vocabulary.translation: 等汤凉了再喝。

vocabulary.entry: overheat /ˌəʊvəˈhiːt/ v. 过热；变得太热
vocabulary.example: The car engine overheated on the long drive in the sun.
vocabulary.translation: 在阳光下长途行驶，汽车发动机过热了。

vocabulary.entry: drowsy /ˈdraʊzi/ adj. 昏昏欲睡的；困倦的
vocabulary.example: The warm room made her feel drowsy after lunch.
vocabulary.translation: 午饭后，温暖的房间让她感到昏昏欲睡。

vocabulary.entry: exhausted /ɪɡˈzɔːstɪd/ adj. 筋疲力尽的；疲惫不堪的
vocabulary.example: She was exhausted after working for 12 hours straight.
vocabulary.translation: 连续工作12小时后，她筋疲力尽。

vocabulary.entry: nap /næp/ n. 小睡；打盹
vocabulary.example: I like to take a short nap in the afternoon to refresh myself.
vocabulary.translation: 我喜欢在下午小睡一会儿，恢复精神。

vocabulary.entry: automatic /ˌɔːtəˈmætɪk/ adj. 无意识的；自动的
vocabulary.example: Breathing is an automatic process that we don’t have to think about.
vocabulary.translation: 呼吸是一个无意识的过程，我们无需刻意去想。

vocabulary.entry: cognitive behaviour /ˌkɒɡnətɪv bɪˈheɪvjə(r)/ 认知行为
vocabulary.example: The study focuses on how cognitive behaviour is influenced by social factors.
vocabulary.translation: 这项研究关注认知行为如何受到社会因素的影响。

vocabulary.entry: identify with /aɪˈdentɪfaɪ wɪð/ 认同；与……产生共鸣
vocabulary.example: Many readers identify with the main character in the novel.
vocabulary.translation: 很多读者都能与小说中的主角产生共鸣。

vocabulary.entry: exhibit /ɪɡˈzɪbɪt/ v. 表现出；展示
vocabulary.example: The child exhibited signs of anxiety before the exam.
vocabulary.translation: 这个孩子在考试前表现出焦虑的迹象。

vocabulary.entry: resist /rɪˈzɪst/ v. 抵抗；抗拒
vocabulary.example: She tried to resist the temptation to eat the cake.
vocabulary.translation: 她试图抗拒吃蛋糕的诱惑。

vocabulary.entry: urge /ɜːdʒ/ n. 强烈的欲望；冲动
vocabulary.example: He felt a sudden urge to travel around the world.
vocabulary.translation: 他突然有了环游世界的强烈冲动。

vocabulary.entry: electrical stimulation /ɪˈlektrɪkl ˌstɪmjʊˈleɪʃn/ 电刺激
vocabulary.example: Electrical stimulation is sometimes used in physical therapy to relieve pain.
vocabulary.translation: 电刺激有时用于物理治疗以缓解疼痛。

vocabulary.entry: Tourette’s syndrome /tʊˈrets sɪndrəʊm/ 图雷特综合征（一种神经系统疾病，表现为不自主的抽搐或发声）
vocabulary.example: Tourette’s syndrome often begins in childhood and can vary in severity.
vocabulary.translation: 图雷特综合征通常在儿童时期发病，严重程度各不相同。

vocabulary.entry: creep up on /kriːp ʌp ɒn/ 不知不觉袭来；悄然发生
vocabulary.example: Old age creeps up on you before you know it.
vocabulary.translation: 衰老会在你不知不觉中悄然降临。

vocabulary.entry: cognitive /ˈkɒɡnətɪv/ adj. 认知的；与认知有关的
vocabulary.example: Cognitive skills such as memory and attention are important for learning.
vocabulary.translation: 记忆和注意力等认知技能对学习很重要。

sentences.chinese: 打哈欠是我们每个人都会做的事——可能是因为我们在做单调乏味的任务时感到无聊，也可能是因为疲惫。

sentences.english: Sometimes, just seeing other people yawn can set you off.
sentences.chinese: 有时候，仅仅看到别人打哈欠你也会跟着打。

sentences.english: But is this biological function really contagious, and why do we do it in the first place?
sentences.chinese: 但这种生理功能真的会传染吗？首先，我们为什么会打哈欠呢？

sentences.english: Many of us think we open our mouths when we yawn to take in more oxygen, but in fact it appears there is no clear biological reason.
sentences.chinese: 我们很多人认为，打哈欠时张大嘴巴是为了吸入更多氧气，但实际上，这似乎并没有明确的生物学原因。

sentences.english: According to BBC Bitesize, new research suggests it might be because yawning cools the brain down and prevents it from overheating, much like the fan in your laptop.
sentences.chinese: 据BBC学习频道（BBC Bitesize）报道，新的研究表明，打哈欠可能是为了给大脑降温，防止其过热，就像你笔记本电脑里的风扇一样。

sentences.english: This might be why we’re more likely to feel drowsy and yawn in warm temperatures.
sentences.chinese: 这或许就是为什么我们在温暖的环境中更容易感到昏昏欲睡并打哈欠的原因。

sentences.english: What is clear is that we yawn more when we’re exhausted and ready for a nap, and we can’t control when we do it – once we start, there’s no stopping us!
sentences.chinese: 可以确定的是，当我们疲惫不堪、准备小睡时，会更频繁地打哈欠，而且我们无法控制打哈欠的时机——一旦开始，就停不下来！

sentences.english: But it’s also true that yawning is a very contagious behaviour.
sentences.chinese: 但打哈欠确实是一种极具传染性的行为。

sentences.english: John Drury, a researcher from Sussex University, told the BBC that “it’s meant to be automatic; it’s something that you can’t stop.
sentences.chinese: 萨塞克斯大学的研究员约翰·德鲁里向BBC表示：“它本来就是无意识的，是你无法阻止的事情。

sentences.english: Dogs yawn when their owners yawn, animals yawn to each other.
sentences.chinese: 主人打哈欠时，狗也会跟着打，动物之间也会相互打哈欠。

sentences.english: It happens whether you want to or not.”
sentences.chinese: 不管你愿不愿意，它都会发生。”

sentences.english: His research into this cognitive behaviour found that there is a connection with our social group and how close we are to the people in it.
sentences.chinese: 他对这种认知行为的研究发现，这与我们的社交圈以及我们和圈内人的亲密程度有关。

sentences.english: If we identify with the person who exhibits the behaviour, we are likely to copy it too.
sentences.chinese: 如果我们认同表现出这种行为的人，就很可能会模仿他们。

sentences.english: Other research by the University of Nottingham in 2017 found similar results.
sentences.chinese: 诺丁汉大学2017年的另一项研究也得出了类似的结果。

sentences.english: They asked volunteers to watch other people yawn. They found their ability to resist yawning when others around them yawned was limited.
sentences.chinese: 研究人员让志愿者观看别人打哈欠的画面，发现他们在周围人打哈欠时，抗拒打哈欠的能力很有限。

sentences.english: And the urge to yawn was increased when people were told they couldn’t.
sentences.chinese: 而且当被告知不能打哈欠时，打哈欠的欲望反而会增强。

sentences.english: They also found, when using electrical stimulation, that they were able to increase people’s desire to yawn.
sentences.chinese: 他们还发现，通过电流刺激，能够增强人们打哈欠的欲望。

sentences.english: These findings, they say, could be useful because it could help treat other conditions like Tourette’s, which involve the same area of the brain.
sentences.chinese: 研究人员表示，这些发现可能很有价值，因为它有助于治疗图雷特综合征等其他疾病——这些疾病涉及与打哈欠有关的大脑的同一区域。

sentences.english: What is certain is that a yawn can creep up on us at any time even when we think we’re not tired – but, I hope, not when you’re reading this article!
sentences.chinese: 可以肯定的是，即使我们认为自己不累，打哈欠的冲动也可能在任何时候不知不觉袭来——不过，我希望你在读这篇文章的时候不会这样！
